title: Comprehension: Follow the Whole Sentence
description: Practice extracting who, number, inclusion, action frame, and time clues from source-checked Hawaiian sentences.

sourceReview.notes: Examples are taken from UH Maui College E Hoʻoulu Lāhui and the modern Reference Grammar of the Hawaiian Language. Activities test interpretation of relationships and context rather than isolated word spotting.

activities.prompt: Do not translate one word at a time.
activities.support: Use the time clue, action frame, and pronoun together.
activities.sentence: I nehinei, e hiamoe ana au i ka hola ʻekolu.
activities.naturalEnglish: Yesterday, I was sleeping at three o'clock.
activities.patternIntro: The sentence gives a past-time clue first, then an e ... ana action frame, then au tells you the speaker is the one doing the action.

parts.label: Action frame
parts.note: sleeping / ongoing action in this context

activities.languageNote: The meaning comes from the combination of clues. e ... ana by itself does not force one English tense; the time expression helps establish context.

activities.prompt: I nehinei, e hiamoe ana au i ka hola ʻekolu.
activities.explanation: au means I, so the speaker is the person sleeping.

activities.prompt: I nehinei, e hiamoe ana au i ka hola ʻekolu.
activities.support: Which word tells you the larger time context?
activities.explanation: I nehinei means yesterday, which anchors the ongoing action in past context.

activities.instruction: Read the question as a whole.
activities.prompt: Track both the question and who is being addressed.
activities.support: The pronoun changes how many listeners are included.
activities.naturalEnglish: What will you all be doing?
activities.patternIntro: aha asks what, while ʻoukou tells you the question is addressed to three or more people.

parts.label: Question
parts.note: what will be happening / what will be done in this pattern

activities.languageNote: Recognizing ʻoukou changes the social context of the whole question.

activities.support: How many people is the speaker addressing?

activities.prompt: Notice that one sentence can contain more than one person reference.
activities.support: Do not stop after recognizing Pāpā.
activities.sentence: I koʻu wā kamaliʻi, ke huhū ʻo Pāpā, makaʻu mākou.
activities.naturalEnglish: When I was a child, when Dad gets angry, we are afraid.
activities.patternIntro: This sentence contains the speaker's childhood context, Pāpā as one participant, and mākou as a different group.

parts.label: Context
parts.note: in my childhood / when I was a child

parts.label: Group
parts.note: we — three or more, excluding the listener

activities.languageNote: Understanding the sentence requires tracking that Pāpā and mākou refer to different participants.

activities.prompt: I koʻu wā kamaliʻi, ke huhū ʻo Pāpā, makaʻu mākou.
activities.support: Does mākou include the person being spoken to?
activities.explanation: mākou is first-person plural exclusive, so the listener is not included.

activities.instruction: Apply the pronoun system in a new sentence.
activities.prompt: Ua ʻike ʻo ia iā mākou i ke kula.
activities.support: Who did he or she see?
options: The speaker's group of three or more, excluding the listener
activities.answer: The speaker's group of three or more, excluding the listener
activities.explanation: iā mākou refers to us — three or more including the speaker but excluding the listener.

activities.instruction: Apply the same system after a preposition.
activities.prompt: E hele au me ʻoukou i ke kula.
activities.support: Who will the speaker go with?
options: You all — three or more people
activities.answer: You all — three or more people
activities.explanation: me ʻoukou means with you, addressing three or more people.

activities.instruction: Use context, not a one-word translation.
activities.prompt: E kamaʻilio ana au iā Kimo i nehinei.
activities.support: Why is a past-time meaning appropriate here even though the sentence uses e ... ana?
options: Because nehinei gives a past-time context
Because au always means past tense
Because e ... ana always means past
activities.answer: Because nehinei gives a past-time context
activities.explanation: The reference grammar notes that e ... ana can describe incomplete action in different time frames; surrounding context such as nehinei determines the interpretation.
